clue.text: Tree obscuring a Calais café

indicators.note: obscuring the letters of the phrase disguises them, so they are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A tree blocks the view of a little French café in Calais.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obscuring' signals the anagram of A CALAIS CAFE.
explanation.definitionFit: The false acacia, or black locust, is a North American tree in the pea family.

clue.text: Combination of char, maybe, and carpenter bound to make a British institution

parts.note: char is a kind of fish, given as an example
taken as written
Chips is the traditional nickname for a ship's carpenter
to bound is to hop or leap

explanation.surface: Mixing a cleaning lady with a woodworker somehow produces a national treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'char' reads as a cleaning lady, but it is the fish, and the carpenter is CHIPS, his old naval nickname. A fish-and-chip shop is a British takeaway selling fried fish and chips.
explanation.definitionFit: The fried-fish takeaway is a cherished national fixture, so it counts as an institution.

clue.text: Master film director gets Oscar finally

indicators.note: the director gets a letter put into his name, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: David Lean directed Lawrence of Arabia

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the word Oscar

explanation.surface: A film director finally wins an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gets' puts R, the last letter of Oscar, inside LEAN.
explanation.definitionFit: To master a skill is to learn it thoroughly; both are verbs of acquiring knowledge.

clue.text: Look confrontational

definitions.meaning: to look at someone closely or stare at them

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to stare at; as a modifier, from eyeball-to-eyeball, it describes a tense face-off.

clue.text: Part of United Kingdom Bill overturned creating legal precedent

indicators.note: overturned in a down clue means the combined pieces are turned upside down, read from the bottom

parts.note: Wales is one of the four nations of the UK
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: A piece of Welsh legislation is overturned, setting a precedent in law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overturned' turns WALES + AC as one run, making CASELAW.
explanation.definitionFit: Law built from judges' earlier decisions in cases serves as binding precedent for later courts.

clue.text: Intellectual brain reduced by 60% in Rye, say?

indicators.note: the shortened word sits in the grain word, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: rye is an example of a cereal crop

indicators.note: cutting three of the five letters of the word brain leaves only two

explanation.surface: A clever mind is found to be shrunk by more than half when dosed with rye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reduced by 60%' keeps only the first two of the five letters of the brain word, which go 'in' the grain; 'Rye' looks like the English town but is the crop.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerebral and intellectual are synonyms, both describing activity of the mind rather than emotion.

clue.text: Basic physical attraction of beast on barred property?

parts.note: a beast is an animal
magnetism is the property of a bar magnet, a barred iron

explanation.surface: Raw allure is compared to a beast standing on fenced-off land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'barred property' suggests land behind bars; it is the property found in a bar magnet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means raw personal charisma or sexual allure, the instinctive pull one person has on another.

clue.text: Earth-dweller knocking wings off UFO X-cube

indicators.note: the wings of the phrase are its outermost letters, which are knocked away

explanation.surface: Something living underground knocks the edges off a cube-shaped flying saucer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking wings off' strips the first and last letters of UFOXCUBE, its U and E, leaving the young animal. An earth is a fox's burrow.
explanation.definitionFit: A young fox lives in an earth, the burrow foxes make, so it is a dweller there.

clue.text: See 13
Performing women not allowed to interrupt one

indicators.note: the stag piece breaks into the word one, so it sits inside it

parts.note: a stag party or stag night is for men only

explanation.surface: In a men-only gathering, a performer is cut off mid-act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to interrupt' puts the men-only party inside ONE; 'women not allowed' looks like part of the story but is the stag night.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor who is on stage is performing in front of an audience.

clue.text: Anxious type, dumping wife for siren initially, in a comparatively poor state

indicators.note: dumping one letter for another swaps the first out and puts the second in its place

parts.note: a worrier is someone who frets

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word siren

explanation.surface: A nervous man leaves his wife for a seductress and ends up worse off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dumping' wife 'for' siren replaces W with S in WORRIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrier is the comparative of sorry in the sense of wretched, so it means in a worse condition.

clue.text: Union post for defence against strikes

parts.note: a chain is a union or linking of parts
post and mail both mean letters delivered

explanation.surface: A trade union's newsletter offers protection during industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Union' and 'strikes' suggest labour relations; the strikes are blows from weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: Interlinked metal rings worn by medieval soldiers protected them from sword and axe blows.

clue.text: Funny paper, so vote negatively?

definitions.meaning: read as three words, it is to ..., voting against

explanation.surface: Is a comic paper a reason to vote against something?
explanation.walkthrough: The Beano is a long-running British children's comic. The 'so' is a link, and the second sense splits the word into BE A NO.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beano is a British comic, which is a funny paper; split up it means be a no vote.

clue.text: Stiff rum without hesitation when in love, as personal protection

parts.note: a stiff is slang for a corpse, a dead body

indicators.note: the remaining letter goes inside the word for love

parts.note: amour is French for love, used in English for a love affair

indicators.note: without means the hesitation letters are taken away from the word rum

parts.note: um is a hesitant noise in speech

explanation.surface: A rum-soaked lover who stops dithering seeks protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' takes UM from RUM, leaving R, which goes 'in' AMOUR to make ARMOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Protective clothing worn by soldiers or police shields the wearer's torso from harm.

clue.text: Conservative club embraces rule which facilitates retraction of what one earlier pounded home!

definitions.text: which facilitates retraction of what one earlier pounded home

indicators.note: the Tory club wraps its arms around the rule, so that piece sits inside

parts.note: a club is a heavy weapon like a hammer
a law is a rule

explanation.surface: A Tory club takes up a regulation about pulling out what it once hammered in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraces' wraps the Tory-plus-weapon round the rule. The long definition describes the curved claw used to pull nails back out.
explanation.definitionFit: This hammer has a split, curved claw at the back of its head for pulling out nails already driven in.

clue.text: Means of global communication put inside alien

parts.note: to intern someone is to confine them
ET is the film alien, a crossword stock abbreviation

explanation.surface: A worldwide network is placed inside an extraterrestrial.
explanation.definitionFit: The worldwide network of linked computers is the main channel of global communication today.

clue.text: Where publicans often are 'canned'?

definitions.meaning: landlords serve standing at the back of the counter
slang for imprisoned, in the can

explanation.definitionFit: Publicans work at the rear of pub counters; the phrase also means in prison, as in the can.

clue.text: Garment that could prevent the fatal progress of slugs

definitions.text: Garment that could prevent the fatal progress of slugs

parts.words: Garment that could prevent the fatal progress of slugs
parts.note: slugs suggests garden pests, but here they are ..., and the garment is protective wear that stops them

explanation.definitionFit: A protective vest made to stop gunfire keeps the wearer from being shot dead.

clue.text: Bass before oxygen-enriched April swims of Arctic and Antarctic regions

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for bass in music

indicators.note: the letters swim about, moving into a new arrangement

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A bass fish swims ahead in oxygen-rich spring waters near the poles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swims' scrambles O with APRIL; 'Bass' looks like the fish but is the musical abbreviation, and 'enriched' only links the oxygen to April.
explanation.definitionFit: Bipolar means relating to both poles, north and south, as of the Arctic and Antarctic.

clue.text: Dancing, hard on the tail of eisteddfod's Welsh location

indicators.note: the letters dance about into a new order
the tail of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Dancing hard at the end of a Welsh arts festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dancing' mixes HARD ON with D, the tail of eisteddfod, a Welsh festival of music and poetry. The Rhondda is a former mining valley in South Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rhondda is a valley district in South Wales, so it is a place in Wales.

clue.text: Say nowadays, 'Gosh!'

parts.note: eg, for example, is what say means here
AD, anno domini, marks the present era

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims in surprise, speaking in a modern way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' looks like an instruction to speak; it means for example.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are mild, old-fashioned exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Unidentified male, John, accepts name entered by old-timer

indicators.note: the surname takes in the name label, so that piece goes inside

parts.note: John Doe is the placeholder name for an unidentified man in the US
a tag is a name or label

explanation.surface: An anonymous man called John takes on a name from an elderly person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' puts the label inside the anonymous surname; 'old-timer' looks like the definition but the whole phrase describes the state of old age.
explanation.definitionFit: Dotage is the feeble state of old age, a condition an elderly person enters.

clue.text: Run out, legs extended by a quarter

parts.note: legs of a race are laps
E for east is one of four compass quarters

explanation.surface: Running out of steam, a runner's stages are stretched by a quarter.
explanation.definitionFit: A subscription or policy that lapses comes to an end, which is to run out.

clue.text: See 16 Down
Play soldier moulds

parts.note: play and fun both mean amusement
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A child plays with a toy soldier and shapes it from clay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moulds' looks like a verb; it is the plural noun, growths of fungus.
explanation.definitionFit: Moulds are a kind of fungus, so fungi covers them.

clue.text: Intoxicant has the drunk taking one look back

indicators.note: drunk means the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: an means one

indicators.note: back means the word for look is read in reverse

parts.note: lo is an old word for look

explanation.surface: A drink takes hold of a drunk, who glances behind him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' gives ETH from THE and 'back' turns LO into OL.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethanol is the alcohol in drinks, the substance that intoxicates.

clue.text: Stepping out from pear-shaped can in Row G

indicators.note: the jumbled letters sit in the noisy word, one piece inside the other

parts.note: a row is a din, a noise

indicators.note: gone wrong, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Escaping from a misshapen tin can in a row of seats labelled G.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pear-shaped' makes ANC from CAN, which goes 'in' DIN + G. 'Row' looks like a seating line; it is noise.
explanation.definitionFit: Stepping out can mean dancing, moving one's feet in time.

clue.text: Regulatory nature of the father of parliaments abroad

indicators.note: abroad means spread about, so the letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: A remark about the controlling character of Westminster, the mother of parliaments, viewed from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'father of parliaments' plays on Westminster's nickname 'mother of parliaments'.
explanation.definitionFit: Paternalism is a policy of controlling people as a father would, supposedly for their own good.
